full_judgment:
This present petitioners, as preemptors, filed the Miscellaneous Case No.18 of 2005 in the court of Assistant. Judge, Narshingdi for preemption under Section 24 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act stating, inter alia, that they were co-sharer of the case holding; that the opposite party No. 4, Without serving any notice to them, sold the land under preemption to the opposite party No.1, but instead of executing sale deed he executed a deed of exchange only to defeat the right of preemption of the petitioners; that the said purchaser was a stranger to the case holding. 

 3. The purchaser Depali Roy Depti contested that preemption case by filing written objection making statements to the. effect that she did not purchase the land in question, rather she got that land by exchange with her some other land and that the transfer deed was thus duly prepared as a. deed of exchange and in the said deed of exchange both the lands thus exchanged were described in schedule "Ka" and "Kha". That she and opposite party No.4 Sree Adhir Dutta also got the delivery possession of their respective exchanged lands and she has already constructed her residential huts in that land; that since the land was not sold rather was exchanged with another land within the same municipality of Gorashal the preemption proceeding under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 was not maintainable. 

 4. The trial Court, on consideration of the evidence, adduced by both the parties rejected the prayer for preemption finding that the transaction between the parties was nothing but exchange. The appellate Court below reversed the judgment of the trial Court and allowed the preemption. In revision the High Court Division set aside the judgment of the appellate.. Court below and restored the judgment of the trial Court on making findings and observations to the effect that the  transaction between the parties was nothing but exchange and that such exchange of land within a municipality area was not preemptable under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. 

 7. We find that the High Court Division, on proper assessment and appreciation of the evidence on record, has rightly found that the transaction between the parties was nothing but exchange and as such this preemption under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural .Tenancy Act was not maintainable.
